title: Ice Sheets in Retreat
objective: After this level you can explain how Greenland and Antarctica are losing ice and why their slow response matters for centuries.
summary: Satellites show Greenland and Antarctica losing ice since 2002 through surface melt and outlet glaciers. Both are committed to losses for decades or centuries.

cards.headline: Satellites can weigh an ice sheet from space.
cards.body: Since 2002, the GRACE satellites, short for Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment, have tracked the ice on Greenland and Antarctica. Both scales read in the same direction.

cards.headline: Two giants losing weight
cards.body: Earth's two ice sheets cap Greenland and Antarctica. Since 2002, Greenland has lost roughly 260 billion tons of ice a year and Antarctica roughly 135 billion. That's ice you could never see go from a beach chair, but the satellites keep the books.

cards.headline: Melting from above and at the edges
cards.body: The ice goes in two main ways. In Greenland, the surface melts in summer, and the IPCC finds human influence has very likely contributed to that melting over the past two decades. At the edges of both sheets, large outlet glaciers carry ice to the sea, and warming ocean water near them plays a key role in the losses. For Antarctica, evidence of the human part is still limited.

cards.headline: A slow, long commitment
cards.body: Ice sheets respond slowly, and they keep responding. The IPCC says glaciers are committed to keep melting for decades or centuries: continued ice loss this century is virtually certain for Greenland and likely for Antarctica. The pace is the open question. Rare instabilities, some involving tipping points, could sharply speed Antarctic losses under high emissions, but their odds carry deep uncertainty.

cards.headline: Ice sheets: tracked
learned: GRACE satellites weigh the ice sheets
Surface melt and outlet glaciers drive losses
Losses continue for decades or centuries

questions.prompt: Match each with its fact from the satellite record.
questions.explanation: Since 2002, Greenland has lost roughly 260 billion tons of ice a year and Antarctica roughly 135 billion, as tracked by GRACE, the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment.

questions.prompt: Imagine global warming stopped tomorrow. Based on the IPCC's assessment, what would the ice sheets most likely do?

options.label: Keep losing ice for decades or longer
Start growing back within a few years
options.rationale: Glaciers are committed to keep melting.

options.label: Stop melting the very next summer
options.rationale: Ice sheets respond slowly, for centuries.

options.label: Vanish completely within a decade
options.rationale: The losses play out over a much longer time.

questions.explanation: Glaciers and ice sheets are committed to keep melting for decades or centuries because they respond slowly.

questions.prompt: Level 2 said ice is a mineral but liquid water isn't. When Greenland's surface ice melts, what happens to that water?

options.label: It stays a mineral, since it is still water
options.rationale: Liquid water fails the solid test.

options.label: It stops being a mineral but stays in the hydrosphere
It leaves the hydrosphere and joins the geosphere
It stops being part of any sphere
options.rationale: All water belongs to the hydrosphere.

questions.explanation: Melted ice is liquid, so it is no longer a mineral, but liquid water, vapor and ice all belong to the hydrosphere.
